title: the word you already say
hookLine: said at good news and bad, all day, at home; the word Sikhs say for God, and it means "wow, the teacher"
tomorrow: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal

cards: Good news on the phone: Waheguru. Someone stands up after sitting on the floor too long: Waheguru. Hard news, said softer: Waheguru.
In many Sikh homes it's said all day long, and hardly ever translated. It turns out to be a name for God built from the smallest word people say when something is bigger than they are.

teach.b: Break it in two. Wahe: wow, wonderful, the cry of amazement. Guru: the teacher, the one who leads from darkness into light.
So Waheguru is something like: wow, the teacher. Notice what kind of name that is.

It isn't a title, like king or judge. It's a reaction. Sikh scripture speaks of a God beyond counting and beyond description, so instead of a description, the name is a response: when words run out, you say wow.

teach.h: THE SAME WORD FOR JOY AND GRIEF.
teach.b: That's why the same word fits joy, relief and grief. It isn't reporting how you feel. It's pointing past the feeling, to what's bigger.
It's the word Sikhs repeat in meditation, slowly, on the breath.

And it's inside the greeting Sikhs trade: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa, the community of committed Sikhs, belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. Ji is a small word of respect, like dear.
So the word you've heard all your life carries a whole idea: wonder isn't only a mood. It's a way of paying attention. And no Punjabi needed here: every word on this path comes with what's inside it.

how: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in meditation, often slowly with the breath, say it in everyday moments of joy or difficulty, and greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh."

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the teacher who leads into light

s: Waheguru is a name that describes what God looks like
Sikhs speak of God as without form. the name is a response of wonder, not a description.
Waheguru is part of the everyday Sikh greeting
Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory.
Sikhs only say Waheguru inside a gurdwara
it's said in meditation, at good news and bad, and in greeting: all through the day.

games.q: you want a name for a God the scripture says can't be counted or measured. what kind of word do you choose?
o: a title, like king or judge.
a cry of wonder: wow, the teacher.
games.why: Waheguru: wahe, wow, and guru, the teacher. when words run out, the name is a response.

practice: One breath with the bell. Look at something near you: your hand, a window, a cup. Breathe in and look at it as if you'd never seen one before.
On the way out, if you like, let the word go with the breath, aloud or silently: Waheguru. Wow.

wordCard.voice: Waheguru. Wahe, wow; guru, the teacher. The name Sikhs say for God, made of wonder. First word on your strand.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: wahe (wonderful, wow) + guru (teacher, enlightener).

carryVoice: Your line: wow. It's the whole name, said the way it feels, and now you know what's inside it. See you tomorrow.
